newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam unlikely to widen forex band - central bank.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam unlikely to widen forex band - central bank.

text.p: Vietnam is most unlikely to further widen the interbank trading band for its currency against the dollar, the director of the State Bank of Vietnam's Foreign Exchange Department said in an interview published on Thursday.
"The State Bank will maintain stability within the band of five percent because our goal is to stabilise the foreign exchange rate," Nguyen Doan Hung told the Vietnam Economic Times.

Six weeks ago the central bank, bowing to persistent demand for the U.S. currency, prised open the official trading band for the Vietnamese dong to five percent either side of its daily indicative rate from one percent.
Shortly after that, the dong moved to its new floor against the dollar and has remained there ever since. On Thursday, the bank's indicative rate was 11,102 per dollar, which put the floor at 11,657.
Asked if the band might be widened again, Hung said: "I think it's most unlikely to happen."
He said the authorities would not allow any sharp fluctuations of the dong and warned that the central bank was capable of intervening in the market.

Denying that the move to widen the trading band reflected a policy of devaluation, Hung said the new regime suited commercial banks better because it brought more flexibility and allowed supply and demand to be properly reflected in the market.
He said the market had now returned to normal after a period of illiquidity and an average of $30-40 million was being traded every day.
Hung said that despite strong economic growth and rising foreign direct investment, the country was now facing serious problems from a trade deficit and debts arising from deferred letters of credit.
A recent government report put the 1996 trade deficit at a record $3.9 billion, around 16 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
Hung said the volume of overdue debts arising from letters of credit, many of which were opened last year when borrowers looked abroad for cheap funds, stood at $1.0 billion.
